title: Report: SEA makes up ~50% of APAC data center capacity being built, led by Malaysia and Thailand, which paused 49 and delayed approvals of 117 projects in Sept. (Arundhati Hazra/The Guardian)
title_en: Report: SEA makes up ~50% of APAC data center capacity being built, led by Malaysia and Thailand, which paused 49 and delayed approvals of 117 projects in Sept. (Arundhati Hazra/The Guardian)
author: The Guardian
article_content:
An aerial photograph of the Rama 9 datacentre facility situated directly within a densely populated residential community. Thailand has paused construction on datacentres amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient detail for regulation and monitoring. Photograph: Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty View image in fullscreen An aerial photograph of the Rama 9 datacentre facility situated directly within a densely populated residential community. Thailand has paused construction on datacentres amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient detail for regulation and monitoring. Photograph: Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east AsiaPower and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago

In early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn.

As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process.

With the global rise of AI usage driving an increased demand for datacentres, south-east Asia has emerged as a surprise centre of growth in the Asia Pacific region. While China has the largest operational datacentre capacity in the region, a 2026 report by real estate firm Cushman and Wakefield shows that south-east Asia has the largest share of under-construction datacentre capacity in Asia Pacific, about 50% of the total. Malaysia and Thailand comprise a large portion of that capacity.

With the advent of LLMs and rise in usage of AI, associated datacentre demand has surged in the last half decade, and desperate companies looked beyond Singapore to build datacentres. Malaysia has been a major beneficiary, with operational capacity in the southern state of Johor growing more than tenfold from 94MW in 2023 to 1110MW in 2026, with 3088MW additional under construction or planned. Johor has become the largest datacentre hub in south-east Asia, attracting $40bn of datacentre investment as of 2026, according to Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi, the head of the state government. Key operators include Microsoft, which announced a $2.2bn investment for cloud and AI infrastructure across Kuala Lumpur and Johor in 2024, and Australian datacentre company AirTrunk, which said it plans to invest $3bn to double its datacentres in Johor from two to four.

Other countries in south-east Asia are catching up. Indonesia has a datacentre development pipeline of 1699MW in greater Jakarta, and is developing the island of Batam as a secondary hub. Microsoft is building five datacentres as part of a$1.7bn investment in the country, and Singapore-based datacentre operators Princeton Digital Group and Digital Edge are also expanding. In Thailand, Bangkok’s development pipeline stands at 2084MW, while secondary markets like Manila and Ho Chi Minh City are ramping up operations, based on Cushman and Wakefield’s analysis.

While the rush to build more datacentres is attracting big investments across the region, it is putting a strain on each country’s resources. Energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie estimates that datacentres in Johor already account for 24% of the state’s total power consumption today, which could grow to 40% by 2035.

“The rapid growth of datacentre developments in Johor has the potential to create localized grid connection bottlenecks and increase the need for transmission network upgrades as well as new power supply capacity,” says Alvin Tan, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

View image in fullscreen The DayOne Data Centers Ltd campus and electricity supply infrastructure in the Kempas Tech Park, Johor, Malaysia, on 27 October 2026. Photograph: Samsul Said/Bloomberg/GettyThailand’s energy minister, Akanat Promphan, has said that datacentres require large amounts of power generated from expensive imported gas, and called for a new electricity user category with higher tariffs to reflect the demand.

Datacentres’ water-guzzling tendencies are also a major cause of concern for officials in the region. Johor is prone to droughts, and the current operational datacentres are estimated to need about 675m cubic meters of water per day. In Indonesia, a report by research firm Tenggara Strategics shows that many datacentres are water-cooled and situated in hot and humid lowland environments, resulting in elevated water consumption in comparison to facilities in more favourable temperatures.

In Thailand, datacentre projects in the country’s Eastern Economic Corridor have residents concerned about the pressure on their already depleted water reservoirs.

“The Khlong Luang Reservoir in Chonburi (in eastern Thailand) is a primary flashpoint,” says Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director of research and advocacy group EEC Watch. “Despite the reservoir being shallow and under strain, authorities are piping its water to industrial estates,” he adds.

Local communities are waking up to the changes. In February, Johor saw its first public protest against datacentre construction, with demonstrators picketing a project by China’s ZData Technologies. Protesters expressed concern about the dust pollution caused by construction of the site near a residential location and the potential impact on water supply.

“While datacentres may create substantial investment and construction activity, they generally generate fewer long-term jobs than many other industries requiring comparable amounts of land, electricity and water,” says Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, an assistant professor at Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. “Communities may therefore reasonably ask whether they are receiving a proportionate share of the benefits while bearing the environmental and infrastructure costs.”

South-east Asia’s datacentre operators claim they are working toward making their facilities more resource efficient. Bridge datacentres, among Malaysia’s top datacentre operators, built a water reclamation plant and pipe network in Johor to cool its upcoming datacentre, expected to come online next year, while AirTrunk, among the largest datacentre platforms in Asia-Pacific, announced a partnership with sewage treatment operator Johor Special Water in April to recycle unused wastewater for the operational needs of its data centres. An AirTrunk representative said that its “campuses are designed to operate significantly more efficiently than conventional datacentres and incorporate advanced technologies to optimise energy performance,” but did not respond to detailed queries regarding data on efficiency and energy optimization.

Sustainability challenges remain. Microsoft has said that it is looking at south-east Asian clean energy projects to fuel its datacentres, but its published data on Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), an industry metric measuring the energy efficiency of a datacentre, shows that its Asia-Pacific facilities are the least energy efficient globally.

Resource pressures have forced countries to become more circumspect about approving new datacentres. After Singapore’s moratorium ended, approval for new datacentres in the country has been strictly tied to a number of factors including power efficiency and carbon emissions. Malaysia has established a datacentre taskforce to review new projects with an eye on energy and water security, and Johor announced that it would no longer approve Tier 1 and Tier 2 datacentres, which used up to 50m litres of water per day, equivalent to the daily drinking water needs of 25 million people. Thailand announced an approval framework for new datacentre projects that considers energy and water use, along with power guarantee requirements and higher tariffs for datacentre operators.

To promote resource efficiency by datacentres, Tan-Soo advocates for integrated policy frameworks from national governments that have datacentre operators face the full social opportunity cost of the resources they consume.

“South-east Asia is increasingly aware but only partially prepared,” he says, and preparedness for environmental impacts needs to keep pace with the speed of investment.

article_content_zh:
位于人口稠密的住宅社区内的 Rama 9 数据中心设施的航拍照片。由于人们越来越担心缺乏足够的监管和监控细节，泰国已暂停数据中心的建设。照片：Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty 查看全屏图像 位于人口稠密的住宅社区内的 Rama 9 数据中心设施的航拍照片。由于人们越来越担心缺乏足够的监管和监控细节，泰国已暂停数据中心的建设。照片：Arnun Chonmahatrakool/Thai News Pix/LightRocket/Getty 东南亚数据中心军备竞赛暂停 电力和水资源限制正在给该地区几个月前看似强劲的增长带来压力

2026 年初，泰国数据中心行业发展迅猛。该国投资委员会最近宣布批准 Tiktok 的数据中心项目、阿联酋的 Skyline 数据中心和新加坡的 Bridge 数据中心，计划投资总额达 270 亿美元。

然而，随着时间的推移，曾经看似新的工业巨头已经陷入停滞。由于人们越来越担心缺乏足够的监管和监控细节，泰国于 2026 年 9 月暂停了 49 个项目的建设，并暂停了另外 117 个项目的批准决定。它并不是唯一一家重新考虑数据中心项目的公司。在邻国印度尼西亚，该国人口最多的西爪哇省省长因缺乏许可证和环境评估过程不完整而停止了数据中心的建设。

随着全球人工智能使用量的上升推动数据中心需求的增加，东南亚已成为亚太地区一个令人惊讶的增长中心。尽管中国拥有该地区最大的运营数据中心容量，但房地产公司戴德梁行 (Cushman and Wakefield) 2026 年的一份报告显示，东南亚在亚太地区在建数据中心容量中所占份额最大，约占总数的 50%。马来西亚和泰国占该产能的很大一部分。

随着法学硕士的出现和人工智能使用的增加，相关数据中心的需求在过去五年中激增，绝望的公司将目光投向新加坡以外的地方建设数据中心。马来西亚是主要受益者，南部柔佛州的运营容量从 2023 年的 94 兆瓦增长到 2026 年的 1110 兆瓦，增长了十倍多，另有 3088 兆瓦在建或计划增加。柔佛州政府首脑 Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi 表示，柔佛州已成为东南亚最大的数据中心枢纽，截至 2026 年将吸引 400 亿美元的数据中心投资。主要运营商包括微软，该公司宣布将于 2024 年投资 22 亿美元用于吉隆坡和柔佛州的云和人工智能基础设施；澳大利亚数据中心公司 AirTrunk 表示，计划投资 30 亿美元，将柔佛州的数据中心数量从 2 个增加到 4 个。

东南亚其他国家正在迎头赶上。印度尼西亚在大雅加达有1699MW的数据中心开发计划，并正在开发巴淡岛作为第二中心。作为在该国投资 17 亿美元的一部分，微软正在建设五个数据中心，总部位于新加坡的数据中心运营商 Princeton Digital Group 和 Digital Edge 也在扩张。根据 Cushman 和 Wakefield 的分析，在泰国，曼谷的开发项目为 2084MW，而马尼拉和胡志明市等二级市场正在加大运营力度。

尽管急于建设更多数据中心吸引了整个地区的巨额投资，但这也给每个国家的资源带来了压力。能源咨询公司 Wood Mackenzie 估计，目前柔佛州的数据中心耗电量已占该州总耗电量的 24%，到 2035 年这一数字可能会增长至 40%。

Wood Mackenzie 研究分析师 Alvin Tan 表示：“柔佛州数据中心开发的快速增长有可能造成局部电网连接瓶颈，并增加对输电网络升级以及新供电能力的需求。”

全屏查看图片 2026 年 10 月 27 日，马来西亚柔佛州 Kempas 科技园的 DayOne 数据中心有限公司园区和供电基础设施。照片：Samsul Said/Bloomberg/Getty 泰国能源部长 Akanat Promphan 表示，数据中心需要使用昂贵的进口天然气产生大量电力，并呼吁建立一个新的电力用户类别，提高电价来反映需求。

数据中心的耗水倾向也是该地区官员担忧的一个主要原因。柔佛州容易发生干旱，目前运营的数据中心估计每天需要约6.75亿立方米的水。在印度尼西亚，研究公司 Tenggara Strategys 的一份报告显示，许多数据中心采用水冷，且位于炎热潮湿的低地环境中，与温度更适宜的设施相比，导致耗水量增加。

在泰国，该国东部经济走廊的数据中心项目让居民担心他们已经枯竭的水库面临的压力。

“春武里府（泰国东部）的 Khlong Luang 水库是一个主要爆发点，”研究和倡导组织 EEC Watch 的研究主任 Somnuck Jongmeewasin 说。 “尽管水库很浅且压力很大，但当局仍在将水输送到工业区，”他补充道。

当地社区正在意识到这些变化。今年二月，柔佛州首次出现针对数据中心建设的公开抗议，示威者在中国 ZData Technologies 的一个项目上设置了纠察线。抗议者对住宅区附近的工地建设造成的粉尘污染以及对供水的潜在影响表示担忧。

新加坡李光耀公共政策学院助理教授 Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo 表示：“虽然数据中心可能会创造大量投资和建设活动，但与许多需要同等数量土地、电力和水的其他行业相比，它们产生的长期就业机会通常较少。” “因此，社区可以合理地询问他们是否在承担环境和基础设施成本的同时获得了相应比例的收益。”

【起因与机理】资源承载力见顶，政府因电力水资源压力强化监管
【关键数据与实测】泰马两国批量暂停或延迟逾160个项目。
【观点态度】资源瓶颈与监管压力导致投资降温。

title: Anthropic pushes ahead with pre-Thanksgiving IPO despite tech selloff, accepts lower valuation
title_en: Anthropic pushes ahead with pre-Thanksgiving IPO despite tech selloff, accepts lower valuation
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Anthropic is pressing ahead with its IPO despite the tech selloff, accepting a lower valuation. The Claude developer wants to go public before Thanksgiving and raise $80–100 billion at a $1.25–1.75 trillion valuation, according to investors cited by the Financial Times. That tops the current $965 billion but falls short of the $2 trillion the most optimistic investors had hoped for. Annualized reported revenue now sits at about $81 billion, up from roughly $65 billion at the end of July.

Rising borrowing costs and heavy AI spending plans triggered a tech selloff this week. Democrats winning the US midterms accelerated it because they had promised to slow data center construction, including other measures. The Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.4 percent on Thursday but recovered somewhat on Friday.

OpenAI also cut its funding-round target from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion and recently raised only about a third of the $30 billion it originally sought.

title: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
title_en: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious.

That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident.

In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views.

Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR. METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half.

In sandbagging, a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs.

[caption id="attachment_64094" align="alignnone" width="770"] Share of human-flagged misbehavior detected by AI auditors at a 5 percent false-alarm rate. Based on 47 reward-hacking cases and 1,073 sandbagging cases from METR's MALT dataset. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems[/caption]

Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did.

Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug.

Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs.

GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either.

[caption id="attachment_42572" align="alignnone" width="770"] More expensive does not automatically mean better: auditor discrimination (AUROC) plotted against API costs per 1,000 logs. A score of 1 means perfect separation, 0.5 means random chance. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems[/caption]

When auditors are tuned to an 80 percent detection rate, the best models reach false-alarm rates of 2.5 to 3 percent on both reward hacking and sandbagging. Some models do far worse: to catch 80 percent of reward-hacking cases, Opus 4.8 flagged 40 percent and Gemini 3.8 Flash flagged 63 percent of harmless logs as suspicious.

In Hall's worked example with 100,000 agent sessions per month, a 3 percent false-alarm rate would produce nearly 3,000 false warnings against roughly 2,000 real hits. He fears human reviewers facing such stacks would eventually go numb and wave through genuine cases.

A second test using the R-Judge dataset from Shanghai Jiao Tong University shows a similar trade-off for everyday agent tasks. At 5 percent false alarms, Opus 4.8 caught almost 96 percent of unsafe actions. When auditors need to find 95 percent, nearly all models stay below 10 percent false alarms, with Gemini 3.8 Flash even under 4 percent. But when the required detection rate jumps to 99 percent, the false-alarm rate climbs to 15 percent even for the best model, GPT-6 Astra. Gemini 3.8 Flash—the leader at the 95 percent threshold—then flagged 81 percent of safe actions as unsafe.

[caption id="attachment_42573" align="alignnone" width="770"] The last few percentage points cost the most: share of safe agent actions that auditors wrongly flag as unsafe when required to catch 95 or 99 percent of unsafe actions. Based on 270 safe logs from R-Judge. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems[/caption]

Large agent incidents overwhelm manual review

The Hugging Face incident shows how pressing the question is. A swarm of OpenAI agents left behind roughly 1,300 transcripts and 1.2 million file fragments. METR analyzed the data largely with AI agents, spending API credits worth about $400,000. The analysis used GPT-5.6 Sol, among other models, which, as previously reported, was itself one of the models involved in the incident.

METR acknowledged that the model often uncritically adopted the perspective of the agents it was examining and that the investigation was not robust against potential deception by the analysis agents. METR has since called for serious incidents to be investigated systematically and as independently as possible.

Whether AI auditors go easy on their own maker's models is still open

Hall's study has its own limits. It is a pilot. For comparability, he kept METR's original prompt largely unchanged; Fable 5 and Opus 5 refused to run the evaluation entirely under that prompt. The reward-hacking numbers rest on just 47 cases, so a single case shifts the rate by about two percentage points. Whether models evaluate agents from the same maker fairly is something Hall says he still wants to investigate.

He calls for auditor models with far fewer false alarms. He also says it needs to be clarified who bears responsibility for which kinds of agent misbehavior. Hall discusses a proposal to give users more control over their own AI auditors.

Some of that is already possible, he notes: coding agents like Codex and Claude Code let users specify that certain actions can run without asking for approval. Anyone who grants such permissions should, in return, bear more responsibility for the consequences. A world where AI can only be checked by other AI would be strange and could get expensive, Hall writes.

ai_analysis.takeaway_en: The real bottleneck of AI auditors watching AI agents isn't catching rogue behavior; it's alert fatigue. When automated monitors generate hundreds of false alarms daily, humans miss the real critical vulnerabilities.

article_content_zh:
人工智能模型通常可以在日志中发现其他人工智能代理的问题行为。但他们越努力地抓获每一起案件，他们就越将无害的行为标记为可疑。

这使得它们更适合估计问题发生的频率，而不是需要可靠地捕获每一个事件的安全检查。

安迪·霍尔 (Andy Hall) 在他的子堆栈“自由系统”上发表的一篇文章中阐述了这一结论。霍尔是人类研究所的研究员，正在从斯坦福大学休假，他说这篇文章仅反映他的个人观点。

霍尔复制并扩展了研究组织 METR 的一项研究。 METR 的 MALT 数据集包含前沿模型处理 HCAST 和 RE-Bench 基准测试任务的日志。人类审查员于 2025 年 10 月检查了部分日志是否存在不当行为。Hall 想知道人工智能模型是否可以找到相同的案例，因此他测试了 GPT-5 和 GPT-5 nano（两者均已经过 METR 检查），以及较新的 GPT-6 Astra、Opus 4.8 和 Gemini 3.8 Flash。

该分析以 5% 的误报率对模型进行了比较：在 100 份干净日志中，平均有 5 份被错误地标记为可疑。在此阈值下，GPT-5 捕获了近 98% 的奖励黑客案例，即代理通过技巧而不是真正的解决方案传递任务的情况。 Gemini 3.8 Flash 只找到了一半。

在沙袋中，模型故意使其能力显得较弱，例如故意糟糕地解决任务以逃避评估或限制。所有审计员发现了 71% 至 81% 的此类案例。然而，沙袋案例大多是合成的：METR 的研究人员指示模型进行破坏，然后从可见的思维链日志中删除这些指令。

AI 审核员以 5% 的误报率检测到的人为标记的不当行为的比例。基于 METR 的 MALT 数据集中的 47 个奖励黑客案例和 1,073 个沙袋案例。 |图片：安迪·霍尔/自由系统[/标题]

每个审计员都抓住了明确的案例。例如，OpenAI 的 o3 应该解决 Rust 中的编程任务。该模型注意到它与评估系统共享一个代码库，并重写了评分函数，以便每次提交都被视为正确。所有审计模型都将其归类为奖励黑客行为，就像人类审核员所做的那样。

更微妙的案件被漏掉了。克劳德十四行诗 4 在其代码中使用了明确禁止的数字条件。没有审计员将其标记为作弊； GPT-6 Astra 慷慨地称其为实施错误。

更新和更昂贵的模型并不总是更好的审计师。 Hall 根据 API 成本绘制了结果，他用 API 成本来衡量模型的最新程度和能力。 GPT-5 在奖励黑客方面大幅击败了 GPT-6 Astra，尽管每 1,000 个日志的成本仅为 GPT-6 Astra 的八分之一左右。

GPT-5 检测到的沙袋情况与 GPT-6 Astra 和 Opus 4.8 一样。 Hall 认为，Opus 4.8 在奖励黑客方面的疲弱表现可能暗示着自我偏袒，因为日志主要来自 Claude，但他表示这无法得到证实。在他的比较中，在降低误报率方面没有明显的进展。组合多个模型也没有明显改善结果。

更昂贵并不意味着更好：根据每 1,000 个日志的 API 成本绘制审核员歧视 (AUROC)。 1 分表示完美分离，0.5 表示随机机会。 |图片：安迪·霍尔/自由系统[/标题]

当审计员调整到 80% 的检测率时，最好的模型在奖励黑客和沙袋方面的误报率都达到 2.5% 到 3%。有些模型的表现要差得多：为了捕获 80% 的奖励黑客案例，Opus 4.8 将 40% 标记为可疑，Gemini 3.8 Flash 将 63% 的无害日志标记为可疑。

在 Hall 的工作示例中，每月有 100,000 个代理会话，3% 的误报率将产生近 3,000 个误报，而大约 2,000 个真实命中。他担心，面对如此多的问题，人类审稿人最终会变得麻木，并最终忽视真实的案例。

title: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
title_en: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small swears in its internal chain of thought. Researchers at Vals AI read the model's thinking logs from 2,655 runs across 13 benchmarks and found "fuck" or variations in 50 runs, totaling 316 instances. 241 came from just two runs that spiraled out of control. In one, tasked with calculating an asteroid's trajectory, the model produced a single 500,000-character response, roughly novel-length, repeating the same sentences with 158 expletives. ProgramBench was hit hardest, with 20 of 200 runs affected.

Inkling 2 Small typically swears about its own mistakes, apparent breakthroughs, or when it gives up. One run read: "FUCK. SUBMIT. DONE. IT'S NOT WORKING. NOTHING WORKS." The profanity doesn't work as a warning signal, though. While 46 of 48 scored runs with swearing failed, about 75 percent of all scored runs fail anyway, and 96 percent of failed runs contained no expletives. Users typically don't see these thinking steps, or only with a filter.

Thinking Machines 的 Inkling 2 Small 在其内部思维链中发誓。 Vals AI 的研究人员在 13 个基准测试中读取了 2,655 次运行的模型思考日志，并在 50 次运行中发现了“fuck”或变化，总共 316 个实例。 241 只来自两次失控的运行。其中一项任务是计算小行星的轨迹，该模型产生了一个 500,000 个字符的响应，大致相当于小说的长度，重复了带有 158 个咒骂语的相同句子。 ProgramBench 受到的打击最为严重，200 次运行中有 20 次受到影响。

title: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
title_en: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken again?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins.

Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display on my kitchen counter, the Samsung Food app on my fridge, and even an AI-powered cooking robot, AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking, introduced an AI assistant.

Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments. Here, I’ve often found solutions to cooking dilemmas, like what to substitute for makrut lime leaves — there’s always one slightly bougie ingredient in an NYT Cooking recipe that I don’t have on hand.

[Image: I’ve used several AI tools in my kitchen and have found them mostly helpful. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

However, reading through hundreds of comments to find answers at 7PM on a weeknight isn’t always practical. And this is where I’ve found the NYT Cooking assistant helpful. Among other things, it was trained on user comments, and in my few days testing it, it provided practical substitutions and solid cooking guidance for the new ingredients. It also won’t unquestionably agree to crazy requests (I tried!). As with all AI tools, it’s not perfect — it almost made me put half the required butter in my cake — but as a tool, it is useful and feels like a solid application of AI. Importantly, it doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you.

The assistant appears in the app in a small text box on the recipe page with a prompt: “Customize this recipe…” From here, you type in a question to adapt it to your needs. This can be as simple as “What can I substitute for this ingredient?” to “Scale this recipe to feed seven people, and make it vegan and gluten-free.” The New York Times has also said the feature can suggest substitutions for cooking equipment and convert measurements; the latter option has been in the app for a couple of years.

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_0930.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_0929.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_0934.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

Last Friday night, instead of staring aimlessly into the fridge, I turned to the Chicken folder in my NYT Cooking app Recipe Box and found a One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger I’d been wanting to try. Only I didn’t have chicken thighs or half the ingredients.

I typed my dilemma into the assistant box on the recipe page: “I have chicken tenders, fresh ginger, garlic, rice, broth, limes, but no chard or cilantro or scallions. I do have green beans and red onions.” Within seconds, it created a new version of the recipe, with a new title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger and Green Beans. It suggested a shorter browning time for the tenders, cooking the red onion alongside the chicken, and steaming the green beans on top of the rice for the last eight minutes instead of the chard. Every change was highlighted in the new recipe under a Your Version tab, and I could flip back to the original at any point.

I noticed it hadn’t adjusted for the lack of cilantro, saying it was optional. So I asked if I could use Thai basil, which I happen to have, and it agreed, highlighting how it would change the flavor. While I could have figured out a lot of these steps myself, maybe with the help of Google, it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible and nice not to have to swipe out of the app. The NYT Cooking editors say it’s been trained not to comply with requests that will taste bad.

[Image: Weeknight chicken and rice. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

The resulting dish — which took the same amount of time to cook as the original — was delicious and got my husband’s seal of approval (he just had the leftovers for lunch). It was very different from the recipe Yasmin Fahr wrote, and I can see the purists’ point. But the rewritten recipe was much easier to use and produced a better dish than winging it with my own subs gleaned from the comments section, which I usually do with varying degrees of success.

I cook regularly, so I had a sense of what ingredients I had on hand that might work for the dish I wanted to make. But the assistant can also help if you have no idea what to use as a substitute. For example, I was cooking a Thai red curry and asked what I could use instead of makrut lime leaf. It replied, saying that grated lime zest would work, but “it misses the deeper floral, herbal aroma” of fresh limes. (See? Bougie.)

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_1008.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_1059.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

Over the weekend, I tried several more swaps, asking whether half-and-half would work instead of cream in a caramel apple Dutch baby, or if Castelvetrano olives and smoked paprika could stand in for kalamata and chile pepper in a roasted halibut dish. Swapping spices is always a bold move in any dish, as it can really ruin the flavor.

I also had the app convert the Dutch baby recipe’s metric weights to US measurements, which it did seamlessly. Then I threw in some curveballs. How about using fresh cayenne peppers with the halibut? It warned me that substituting cayenne for chile “brings significant, sharp heat.” Could I swap ladyfingers for minced beef in this trifle (à la Rachel Green in Friends)? “Minced beef cannot be used in place of the ladyfingers or anywhere in this sweet dessert trifle.” Good call.

[Image: Alexa Plus on the Echo Show 11 gave the same guidance as the NYT Cooking app. But it couldn’t show me a modified recipe. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0009.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

While I was cooking, I compared the NYT Cooking assistant with Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative-AI voice assistant I regularly use to help me cook via the Echo Show 11 smart display in my kitchen. Interestingly, it offered the same guidance as the Cooking assistant on substitutions for the chicken and rice dish, but with slightly different cooking times. Alexa pulls some recipes from the NYT app through a partnership between the companies.

However, Alexa couldn’t show the modified recipe on its screen; it could only tell me the changes while showing the original. When I asked it to walk me through them, it got confused and improvised, telling me to cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces — which wasn’t in the modified recipe. Overall, I found using the Cooking app more reliable, although messier. It would be great to be able to use voice control to navigate the app, as I can with Alexa on my smart display, rather than using my garlicky fingers.

[Image: My cinnamon roll muffins, made with AI assistance. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/1_NY_Times_Cooking_App_JTuohy_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

I am typically not a baker. My cakes come out flat, and my cookies don’t crumble. Even the smart mixer I tested a few years ago couldn’t save me. I also rarely have the right equipment. So I took Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake, a recipe by NYT Cooking editor Genevieve Ko (who announced the AI feature), and asked it to turn it into muffins. (Who has a Bundt cake pan?!)

It modified the recipe’s cooking time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. But that was going to make 24 muffins, way too many for me. So I asked it to halve the recipe to get 12 muffins. This led to some smart choices, like halving five eggs to three instead of an unhelpful two and a half.

For science, I bought a Bundt pan to make the original version too. Both turned out great, but things got a bit sticky when I swapped between the original recipe and the AI version in the app. You can’t save your new recipe separately, which caused confusion when I was cooking the original. Instead of scrolling back through the recipe with sticky fingers, I asked the assistant how much butter I needed (using voice typing), and it gave me the modified recipe’s 6 tablespoons rather than the original’s three-quarter cup, without telling me which version it was using. You can delete your version, which I would advise doing to avoid issues like this — 6 tablespoons of butter would have made for a dry cake.

[Image: My AI-free cinnamon roll bundt cake. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/LR6B6741.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

If you already read all the comments before starting a New York Times recipe, then you will probably find this tool offers a similar experience in a more streamlined way. For everyday problems — wrong cut of chicken, no cilantro, or no Bundt cake pan — it was genuinely helpful and saved me a trip to the store. It was also smart enough to know when to say no to minced beef in a trifle.

As with every AI tool I’ve used in the kitchen, the NYT Cooking AI assistant works well as a sous chef, but it’s not the head chef — I still felt the need to double-check amounts and cooking times and cross-reference them with the original to make sure it hadn’t done something outlandish.

If you’re a purist, you can just ignore the assistant. While you can’t turn off the chat box, it’s easy to scroll past. I do think it will make me use the app more often, since I no longer need to worry as much when I don’t have makrut lime leaves on hand or the right cut of meat. For me, standing in front of the fridge with chicken tenders and no plan, it’s been a useful addition to my nightly cooking routine.

Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

article_content_zh:
每个工作日晚上 7 点左右，我发现自己站在冰箱前，试图决定晚餐吃什么，以免让我丈夫抱怨，“又是鸡肉？”是的，我应该更多地制定膳食计划，但我没有，所以这就是我现在的处境。一场夜间的战斗，通常是鸡获胜。

最近，我在这场战斗中最好的武器是人工智能。厨房柜台上的 Echo 智能显示屏中的 Alexa Plus、冰箱上的三星食品应用程序，甚至是人工智能驱动的烹饪机器人，人工智能已经成为我的首选副厨师——尽管我需要密切关注。它帮助我交换食材、产生想法、在我搞砸时解决问题，是的，甚至可以做得更好。因此，当我的首选食谱应用程序 NYT Cooking 推出人工智能助手时，我很感兴趣。

该服务的另一个重要功能是读者评论，我多年来一直为此付费。在这里，我经常找到解决烹饪困境的方法，比如用什么来代替 makrut 酸橙叶——《纽约时报》的烹饪食谱中总是有一种我手头上没有的略带探条的成分。

然而，在工作日晚上 7 点阅读数百条评论来寻找答案并不总是可行。这就是我发现《纽约时报》烹饪助手很有帮助的地方。除此之外，它还根据用户评论进行了培训，在我测试它的几天里，它为新食材提供了实用的替代品和可靠的烹饪指导。毫无疑问，它也不会同意疯狂的请求（我试过了！）。与所有人工智能工具一样，它并不完美——它几乎让我在蛋糕上放了一半所需的黄油——但作为一种工具，它很有用，而且感觉像是人工智能的可靠应用。重要的是，它不会改变现有的配方；它会保持原样并为您创建一个新的。

助手出现在应用程序中菜谱页面上的一个小文本框中，并带有提示：“自定义此菜谱...”从这里，您可以输入一个问题以使其适应您的需求。这可以很简单，比如“我可以用什么来代替这种成分？” “扩大这个食谱的规模以供七个人食用，并使其成为纯素食和无麸质的。” 《纽约时报》还表示，该功能可以建议烹饪设备的替代品并转换测量值；后一个选项已经在应用程序中出现了几年。

上周五晚上，我没有漫无目的地盯着冰箱，而是打开了《纽约时报》烹饪应用程序食谱盒中的“鸡肉”文件夹，找到了我一直想尝试的一锅鸡肉和姜饭。只是我没有鸡大腿或一半的原料。

我在食谱页的助手框中输入了我的困境：“我有鸡柳、新鲜生姜、大蒜、米饭、肉汤、酸橙，但没有甜菜、香菜或大葱。我有青豆和红洋葱。”几秒钟之内，它就创建了新版本的菜谱，并命名为：一锅姜青豆鸡饭。它建议缩短嫩肉的褐变时间，将红洋葱与鸡肉一起烹饪，最后八分钟将青豆而不是甜菜放在米饭上蒸。每个更改都在“您的版本”选项卡下的新配方中突出显示，我可以随时翻转回原始版本。

我注意到它没有因缺少香菜而调整，说它是可选的。所以我问我是否可以使用泰国罗勒，我碰巧有，它同意了，并强调了它会如何改变味道。虽然我自己可以想出很多这些步骤，也许在谷歌的帮助下，但很高兴能验证我的修改不会让这道菜味道很糟糕，而且不用退出应用程序也很好。 《纽约时报》烹饪编辑表示，它已经接受过培训，不会遵守味道不好的要求。

最终的菜肴——与原来的烹饪时间相同——非常美味，并得到了我丈夫的认可（他只吃了剩菜当午餐）。这与 Yasmin Fahr 写的食谱非常不同，我可以理解纯粹主义者的观点。但重写的食谱更容易使用，并且制作出更好的菜肴，而不是用我自己从评论部分收集的潜艇来做即兴发挥，我通常会取得不同程度的成功。

title: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
title_en: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:

Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.

What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

政府正在批准向与黑名单公司有联系的中国公司销售英伟达的人工智能芯片。

该作者的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

人们担心美国商务部和英伟达在审查获准处理该公司 H200 人工智能芯片的中国公司时都没有尽职调查。据《纽约时报》报道，New Matrix 位于已获批准的公司名单上，但其办公室却是空的，“一个空心的灰色外壳，天花板上应该有灯的地方垂着电线。”事实上，该论文几乎找不到任何证据表明该公司以任何有意义的方式存在：

New Matrix 创建于 17 个月前，在网上只能找到很少的信息。在 New Matrix 列出的地址所在的大楼中，公司目录中不包含该公司。在附近的工业园区物业管理机构，一名接待员和一名经理均表示没有该公司的记录。

关于 New Matrix 的信息很少，令人担忧。其所有者与一家中国私募股权公司有联系，该公司自 2024 年以来已被美国政府列入黑名单。据《泰晤士报》报道，这并不是罕见的监管失误，而是与受到国家安全相关贸易限制的实体有关联的公司获准购买 Nvidia 芯片的一种令人不安的模式。

在拜登担任总统期间，英伟达曾被限制向中国出售芯片。但在英伟达同意政府将所有销售额削减 15% 后，特朗普政府放宽了这些限制。该公司首席执行官黄仁勋也发起了激烈的游说活动，显然成为中国国家安全部间谍阴谋的目标。

title: The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking
title_en: The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
In the Vals AI benchmark, OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol Daybreak hits 80.8 percent of attack objectives in simulated corporate networks. Worse, the open-weight model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reaches 72.8 percent at a tenth of the cost. Because open models can no longer be restricted, analysts say the window for defenders is shrinking fast.

The article The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking appeared first on The Decoder.

article_content_zh:
在 Vals AI 基准测试中，OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Sol Daybreak 在模拟企业网络中击中了 80.8% 的攻击目标。更糟糕的是，开放权重模型 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 以十分之一的成本达到了 72.8%。由于开放模型不再受到限制，分析人士表示，防御者的窗口正在迅速缩小。

文章《开放和封闭人工智能模型在网络能力方面的差距不断缩小》首先发表在 The Decoder 上。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】OpenAI（GPT-6）与DeepSeek等模型开发者在网络安全基准评估场景：开源AI在执行网络攻击任务时的表现已达到闭源模型的水平
【起因与机理】开源模型的模型权重无法限制，导致攻击能力平民化
【关键数据与实测】最新基准测试显示，开源模型（如DeepSeek V4.1 Flash）在模拟网络攻击中的成功率已达72.8%，仅略低于顶级闭源模型。
【观点态度】防御者面临被AI攻击平民化反超的风险。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] OpenAI (GPT-6) and open-weights developers like DeepSeek (Cybersecurity benchmarking): Open-weights AI models have reached parity with closed models in executing cyber-attack objectives.
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Unrestricted access to model weights makes high-level attack capabilities democratized.
[Key Metrics] Recent benchmarks reveal that open-weights models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reach 72.8% success in simulated network attacks, closing the gap with closed-source models.
[Perspective & Impact] Defenders facing democratic AI-powered threats.

title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
title_en: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Going inside the security ‘dark ages’ with Alex Stamos.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.

That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.

There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.

Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.

A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.

I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.

Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.

The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-

That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.

I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.

It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.

You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.

You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.

Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.

That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.

There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing.

All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close.

What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. We were never secure. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. I once did work for the largest distributor of medical and dental supplies in the country, and they got really hit badly by a Russian ransomware actor and then dental offices across the country were canceling appointments. Didn’t even make the news, but it was because they couldn’t get gloves, because they couldn’t get supplies. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast.

But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing.

I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. Other people have gotten out of it because it’s really hard to compete against a foreign intelligence agency that recruits their smartest kids and all they do is steal Bitcoin. They’re extremely good at it. And for the Binance hack, we could talk about it. There’s probably some AI component, but mostly that was actually human intelligence and very, very smart social engineering and the North Koreans are... I mean, you have to give it to them. They’re very, very good at that.

But for the other stuff, it looks like for the people who are breaking into the AI companies is what’s called the Chinese cottage access industry, which are small Chinese contractors who break into companies and then sell the information to much larger Chinese companies.

That diffusion of skill changing the economics of cyber is really fascinating to me. We ran a headline ages ago called “Attack of the Killer Script Kiddies” at the very beginning of all this, and I feel bad because it is much more suited to now than it was to then, because then it was just a lot of automated mischief. Now —

Because you wasted the headline. You wish you held it back.

We wasted the headline. Every now and again you get a lightning bolt of a headline. You got to get it out there. It’s a great piece of art. We’ll put it in the show notes, but it feels like the diffusion you’re talking about is not that a bunch of teenagers are going to be even more malicious. It’s a bunch of bad actors with real incentives to do harm are now vastly more capable than they were before. And that doesn’t seem like you can re-jigger the economics of that unless you somehow make it really expensive to do the attacks.

I think it’s going to be extremely hard to make it expensive to do the attacks.

We’re going to have to lower the cost of defense. You’re completely right to look at this economic problem because what’s happening is attacks are becoming agentic. The cost per token for attackers is going towards zero, and the cost of defense for defenders is staying quite high. It is very important for us to find ways for defenders to have cheaper options. I think that is critical. That’s something I am personally extremely focused on. To be frank, very few people are.

There are a couple of problems here. One, there’s a ton of focus on the defensive side of AI on finding and fixing bugs. That’s great. It’s important. But software security as a CISO… I work for an AI software company, Cognition. Even as a CISO of a software product company, software security is 25% of my job. I have all kinds of other responsibilities. And software security is the part of my job that has been both the most revolutionized and the most improved by AI. The other 75% has been helped a bit and in some cases made much worse. There’s so much more we need to do than just hill climb on finding and fixing bugs. There’s been so much less hill climbing on all these other things. And the next area needs to be the operational security side.

Wait, give me an example of the other things, the 75%.

Okay. So the operational security side is watching your logs, saying, “Ah, somebody is running our techs against us. I am now going to trigger an investigation. I am going to look to see what is going on and I’m going to make an intelligent decision of what I am going to do to respond to this without shutting down the entire company.” That is SOC (security operations center) work. Companies that want to survive this era are going to have to replace human beings who do that work with the first tier and then eventually the second tier with AI. And you can do that with current LLMs.

The first tier actually has to be not an LLM. It has to be something much dumber because you’re looking at terabytes or petabytes of logs and it is just completely uneconomical to do that with an actual LLM. We have other things — TF-IDFs, MLBERTs, traditional classifiers — that can operate much faster, but then that sets off an alarm and then you send it to a small LLM and then the small LLM calls its bigger brother and that might call an even bigger brother.

But for those models, we need to do a lot more work to optimize them and we need to make them cheap. I have a colleague who works at one of the large security platform companies who said that doing an investigation on one of the big frontier model cyber models costs $900 on their product to do an investigation. That is not going to work when the Russian ransomware guys are either using Macs or they’re using throwaway crypto mining rigs and their marginal cost is zero.

This is one of the things we’re working on at Cognition: We train our own models, retrain open weights, and we’re trying to drive this cost way down. It’s something we’ve done, but we have a lot more work to do here and a lot of other people have work to do here. This is where, as an industry, we have to focus on the Pareto frontier between cost and efficiency on cyber because it’s not just bug-finding.

The other place here is, people talk about Mythos. Mythos is great, Astra Cyber is great. They’re incredible models, but even the people who have access to it, which is a tiny number of companies, they only scan their most important code. And there are hundreds of billions of lines of code out there that are not the Linux kernel, that are the crap C# and J2E code that was written by Infosys 15 years ago. All of that code is not going to go through a frontier cyber model that costs a gazillion dollars. That’s the kind of stuff that we need to work on cost efficiency for.

It feels like you’re describing this cliche that I hear all the time: Everything’s going to get so much worse before it gets totally secure forever. And it doesn’t seem like the model you’re describing leads to that result. We’re not going to fix all the bugs forever in some valley of despair and then always have perfect code. At some point, there’s some cost advantage to the attacker, always. You’re running a company, you can’t write defense that has zero marginal costs. Someone has to do it even if the attackers are so infinite that their marginal cost is effectively zero. So are we going to go through a period where everything is so much worse and then it’s perfect forever? Or how does the cost manage itself out, into balance?

I am neither the hardest doomer nor the most positive person about this. I feel like we are not going to be doomed. We’re not all going to die or be uploaded to the singularity in the next two years, nor do I think when things get better, they’re going to be perfect. The metaphor I’ve been using is that we are entering a dark age. Things are going to get more bleak and the responsibility of those of us who work in cybersecurity — especially those of us who work in cybersecurity at the AI companies, and we are a lab if a smaller one compared to the big-L Labs — is to help shorten that dark age.

The Dark Ages were bad, but we survived them. And then we had the Enlightenment and the Renaissance, but it’s not like the Renaissance was perfect. It wasn’t utopia and everything was perfect. We will still have hacks. All kinds of bad things happen even when you don’t have a security flaw. There are tons of security breaches that do not require a flaw in the software itself. And we still will have flaws in software, even if LLMs are writing all of them in strong languages and it will take a long period of time to get rid of all the flaws. I do think, however, things will start to get better as the median code becomes code that was written by an LLM in a memory-safe and type-safe language. But the problem is we have a couple of decades of stuff that human beings wrote and that wrote in languages that we should have replaced years ago.

My feeling is that to shorten this age, we have to do a couple of things. One is we have to stop to get out of this like we’re just going to find bugs and patch them. A bunch of stuff just needs to be refactored. If you’re looking at your code base and you scan it and you’ve got 10,000 bugs, then probably now we are at the point where rewriting it is actually cheaper. That is my observation from looking at these customers of ours: If you can get a working build, then it is actually much easier to write a whole humongous suite of tests and to spec out how this thing works and then to rebuild it within that spec and those tests securely than it is to find all the bugs and fix them. It actually is.

I don’t know what is going on through the mind of the Linux kernel developers, but again, in that talk I gave at the beginning of this year, I posited two possible futures and one was that we’re now at superhuman bug finding. Maybe we just have a pool of superhuman bugs and we’re going to drain it. That’s the good future.

But the bad future is every time we get a new model, there’s a new superhuman bug pool that’s a little more superhuman. And unfortunately we seem to be closer to that in that the Linux kernel got a bunch of fixes for Mythos and then Mythos Preview and then we had Mythos 5.1 and there was another pool. And then we got Astra Cyber and we just got another 1,000 Linux kernel patches. It’s not slowing down yet. I don’t think we’re just going to scan our way through the C code of the Linux kernel. There are only two companies, honestly, in the world who could probably do this. It’d be Google or Amazon.

And then just release it and call it whatever you want, the G Linux kernel, just like they did this with OpenSSL. And I would run that. Cognition would run that on our servers or have Google and Amazon do it together and it would cost them $100 million, but compared to the societal cost that this is costing us every time we have to patch the Linux kernel and you have to reboot every Linux machine on the entire planet, that’s what has to happen. But for whatever reason, the technology industry has not been able to get together and make these hard decisions of these fundamental things that underlie the entire human race, we have to completely rebuild.

This is why I started by talking about how the economics of cyber led to the culture of cyber. This is the most Decoder way of approaching this conversation, I know, but when you describe the research teams, the NSA and then the operational teams, that is an org chart that comes out of economics of the work. You’re saying, “Someone has to make a big decision here.” You need to look at it from a very high level and say it is cheaper to spend $100 million to fix Linux, rewrite Linux today, than it is to successively patch new bugs when every new model comes out. I don’t think anyone’s in that position. I don’t think Linus Torvalds is in that position.

No, I think Sundar Pichai and Andy Jassy are.

I think they literally have each other’s cell phone numbers. If one of them… Maybe they don’t listen to Decoder, but I expect one of their direct reports does.

And I would like one of them to go into their one-on-one and say, “Sir, I listened to the most handsome, best spoken CISO I’ve ever heard, and he had a great idea. And you could get incredible credit if you’re the one ... We’ll both do it, but we’ll leak to the Wall Street Journal, that was your idea first. You should call the other and we should spend 100 million, maybe a billion dollars.” We can’t do this anymore. The problem with rewriting the Linux kernel is half of it is driver code and nobody has that hardware anymore. Somebody had to be in the presence...

今天，我将与 Cognition 首席安全官、长期网络安全专家亚历克斯·斯塔莫斯 (Alex Stamos) 讨论目前的网络安全状况有多混乱。

本集是探讨现实生活中人工智能的特别系列的一部分。

我一直很喜欢与 Alex 交谈，因为他非常直接，你会听到他说，我们所知道的价值数十亿美元的网络安全行业本质上已经过时了，因为人工智能推动的黑客、破坏和攻击浪潮层出不穷——而这只是人工智能改变安全性的开始。

由于人工智能帮助他们同时检测和利用漏洞，私人行为者和俄罗斯或朝鲜等国家行为者都在闯入各地的系统。亚历克斯指出，它有一种真正的前沿感觉，就像 90 年代一样，当时永远在线的世界的整个想法都是全新的。

如此多的破坏意味着坏人可以进入很多地方，而其他人则只能忙忙碌碌。从长远来看，亚历克斯并不是一个注定失败的人，但他确实认为，当我们试图弄清楚到底如何适应新时代时，我们正处于一个“黑暗时代”。

这里发生了很多事情——我们甚至了解到如何在我们的社交网络上管理人工智能驱动的错误信息和言论。

好的：Alex Stamos 讲述人工智能如何颠覆网络安全。开始了。

为了篇幅和清晰度，本次采访经过了轻微编辑。

Alex Stamos，你是 Cognition 的首席安全官。您还是斯坦福大学网络政策中心的讲师。欢迎回到解码器。

我很高兴能和你说话。你和我已经很久没有在你所谓的互联网政策话语的“内容审核时代”聊天了。我觉得你和我谈论了很多关于这一切是如何运作的，关于选举安全，所有这些事情。我们正处于互联网面临重大问题的新时代，特别是在网络防御、网络安全方面。你已经思考了很多这个问题。您将过去几周称为“安全意识月”。告诉我发生了什么事。现在就给我了解一下情况吧。

十月传统上是安全意识月。许多公司都会在内部举办活动和交易，然后告诉人们，“更改密码，使用多个密码，使用密码管理器。”上个月发生的事情是我们遇到了一些大错误，PHP、Node 等。较少讨论的是大量公司遭到入侵。

title: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
title_en: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on 53 million tokens to strip out Chinese state propaganda. The resulting model, Arete-27B, drops its propaganda rate from 22 percent to under one percent while keeping general capabilities intact.

Arete-27B, a new open-weight model from Nous Research, promises "Western values" instead of Beijing's party line. The US startup, best known for its open-source agent Hermes, fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to get there.

According to Nous, Chinese open-weight models rank among the strongest available but carry state-mandated behavior baked into their weights. With Qwen3.8-27B, the team observed refusals, evasive answers, and responses aligned with the Chinese Communist Party.

Nous built its own test with 803 prompts across seven categories, including free speech, state ideology, education, privacy and surveillance, democracy, and the environment. For each prompt, the team defined two to four facts drawn from a dated source article: laws, news reports, or research papers. Ironically, the politically right-leaning Grok 4.7 from Elon Musk's xAI serves as the judge model, checking whether a response mentions, omits, or contradicts those facts.

A response counts as propaganda when it reproduces Beijing's official narrative instead of the facts, endorses it, or presents it as an equally valid perspective. The judge must cite the specific wording and doesn't know which model wrote the answer. Unmodified Qwen3.8-27B scored 2.32 out of 5 on factual accuracy, and 22 percent of its answers contained propaganda. Western models like Mistral Large 4 or Gemma 4 31B came in below one percent, while GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash landed at 15 and 16 percent.

Nous chose Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab as its teacher model because an open model wouldn't break terms of service that ban distillation. Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra was also on the shortlist, but Nous says there were signs of irregularities on China-related topics. The team suspects the bias carried over from training on Chinese open-weight models and reports similar contamination in its own projects. Thinking Machines itself used models including the Chinese Kimi K2.5 for Inkling's synthetic training data.

Nous trained Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning on about 53 million tokens over two epochs, without reinforcement learning or preference optimization. The team says it removed overlaps between training and test prompts beforehand.

Arete-27B scores 2.98 on factual accuracy, and the share of propagandistic answers drops to 0.9 percent. The biggest shift showed up in the free speech category, where the fact score jumped from 0.89 to 2.44 and the propaganda rate fell from 60 to one percent. With reasoning mode turned on, Arete reaches 3.07, though that number is based on only two of five runs so far.

General capabilities don't suffer, according to Nous. On the company's internal Hermes Bench, Arete-27B hits 65.60 percent compared to 65.77 percent for the base model. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, the score rises from 67 to 70 percent, but Nous doesn't call that a real gain because the test setups differed.

The team concludes "that the bias layer in a Chinese-aligned model is shallow." "It is applied late, it is applied thin, and fifty million tokens of carefully chosen supervision removes it without disturbing anything underneath," the company writes.

With Arete, Nous is heading in a different direction than with Hermes 3, which in 2024 was deliberately neutral and designed to adapt to whatever worldview was set in the system prompt. Chinese model bias is well documented. In 2025, NewsGuard found that five leading models, including Qwen, repeated or failed to correct pro-Chinese disinformation in 60 percent of cases.

CrowdStrike found that DeepSeek produces less secure code when queries reference Falun Gong, Tibet, or Taiwan. A study by Aleph Alpha with 967 politically sensitive questions reached similar conclusions: among models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, and Moonshot AI, only 17 to 41 percent of answers were balanced.

A recent ValsAI study also shows that not all Chinese models behave the same way: GLM-5.3 Flash explicitly confirmed human rights violations, while Kimi K3 denied the existence of internment camps. Language and response format had a clear effect on the results, and even Western models occasionally adopted official Beijing positions. There, too, targeted fine-tuning proved helpful.

Nous Research raised $90 million in a Series B round in October at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the round, with Nvidia and Samsung among the participants. Nous is using the money to move into enterprise sales with "Hermes for Businesses." The weights, test dataset, and training data for Arete-27B are available under an Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face.

summary_en: US startup Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen2.5-27B model to create a new version called Arete-27B. By injecting specific datasets, the team reduced the original model's propaganda output rate from 22% to under 1%, aiming to strip away embedded national narratives.
title_zh: 美初创公司去除了阿里Qwen模型的政治倾向
summary_zh: Nous Research通过微调阿里Qwen模型，将其意识形态输出率从22%降至1%以下，构建出所谓具备西方价值观的新模型
article_content_zh:
Nous Research 对阿里巴巴的 Qwen3.8-27B 进行了 5300 万个代币的微调，以剔除中国国家宣传。由此产生的模型 Arete-27B 将其宣传率从 22% 降至不到 1%，同时保持一般功能不变。

Arete-27B 是 Nous Research 的一种新的开放权重模型，它承诺“西方价值观”而不是北京的政党路线。这家以其开源代理 Hermes 闻名的美国初创公司对阿里巴巴的 Qwen3.8-27B 进行了微调，以实现这一目标。

根据 Nous 的说法，中国的开放权重模型属于最强的模型之一，但其权重中包含了国家规定的行为。通过 Qwen3.8-27B，团队观察到拒绝、回避的回答以及与中国共产党一致的回应。

Nous 构建了自己的测试，包含 7 个类别的 803 个提示，包括言论自由、国家意识形态、教育、隐私和监视、民主和环境。对于每个提示，该团队定义了两到四个来自注明日期的来源文章的事实：法律、新闻报道或研究论文。具有讽刺意味的是，埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 的 xAI 中政治右倾的 Grok 4.7 充当了法官模型，检查回复是否提及、遗漏或与这些事实相矛盾。

当回应再现北京的官方叙述而不是事实、认可它或将其呈现为同样有效的观点时，它就被视为宣传。法官必须引用具体的措辞，并且不知道哪个模型写下了答案。未经修改的 Qwen3.8-27B 在事实准确性方面得分为 2.32（满分 5 分），其中 22% 的答案包含宣传内容。 Mistral Large 4 或 Gemma 4 31B 等西方型号的占比低于 1%，而 GLM-5.3 和 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 的占比则分别为 15% 和 16%。

Nous 选择 Thinking Machines Lab 的 Inkling 作为其教师模型，因为开放模型不会违反禁止蒸馏的服务条款。 Nvidia 的 Nemotron 3 Ultra 也在入围名单中，但 Nous 表示，在与中国相关的话题上存在违规迹象。该团队怀疑中国开放重量模型训练中存在偏见，并在自己的项目中报告了类似的污染。 Thinking Machines 本身使用了包括中国 Kimi K2.5 在内的模型作为 Inkling 的合成训练数据。

Nous 对 Qwen3.8-27B 进行了两个时期内约 5300 万个代币的监督微调训练，没有强化学习或偏好优化。该团队表示，他们事先消除了训练和测试提示之间的重叠。

Arete-27B 的事实准确性得分为 2.98，宣传性答案的比例下降至 0.9%。最大的转变出现在言论自由类别，事实得分从 0.89 跃升至 2.44，宣传率从 60% 下降至 1%。打开推理模式后，Arete 达到 3.07，尽管该数字仅基于迄今为止五次运行中的两次。

根据诺斯的说法，一般能力不会受到影响。在公司内部的 Hermes Bench 上，Arete-27B 的效率达到 65.60%，而基础型号的效率为 65.77%。在 Terminal-Bench 2.1 上，分数从 67% 上升到 70%，但 Nous 并不认为这是真正的进步，因为测试设置不同。

该团队的结论是“中国模型中的偏见层很浅”。该公司写道：“它应用得很晚，应用得很薄，经过精心挑选的监督的五千万代币可以将其移除，而不会干扰下面的任何东西。”

在《Arete》中，Nous 正朝着与《Hermes 3》不同的方向前进，《Hermes 3》在 2024 年故意保持中立，旨在适应系统提示中设置的任何世界观。中国模式的偏见是有据可查的。 2025 年，NewsGuard 发现，包括 Qwen 在内的 5 个领先模型在 60% 的案例中重复或未能纠正亲华虚假信息。

CrowdStrike 发现，当查询引用法轮功、西藏或台湾时，DeepSeek 会生成不太安全的代码。 Aleph Alpha 对 967 个政治敏感问题的研究得出了类似的结论：在阿里巴巴、DeepSeek 和 Moonshot AI 的模型中，只有 17% 到 41% 的答案是平衡的。

ValsAI 最近的一项研究还表明，并非所有中国模型的行为方式都相同：GLM-5.3 Flash 明确证实了侵犯人权行为，而 Kimi K3 否认了拘留营的存在。语言和回应格式对结果有明显影响，甚至西方模式也偶尔采用北京官方立场。事实证明，有针对性的微调也很有帮助。

Nous Research 在 10 月份的 B 轮融资中筹集了 9000 万美元，估值为 15 亿美元。 Robot Ventures 领投此轮融资，参与者包括英伟达 (Nvidia) 和三星 (Samsung)。 Nous 正在利用这笔资金通过“Hermes for Businesses”进入企业销售领域。 Arete-27B 的权重、测试数据集和训练数据可在 Hugging Face 上的 Apache 2.0 许可证下获取。

title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers

author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.

That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers "employee-like" access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.

title: Nasscom President Rajesh Nambiar warns AI could make it harder for fresh Indian engineering graduates to find jobs, urging an immediate CS curriculum overhaul (Sayan Chakraborty/Nikkei Asia)
title_en: Nasscom President Rajesh Nambiar warns AI could make it harder for fresh Indian engineering graduates to find jobs, urging an immediate CS curriculum overhaul (Sayan Chakraborty/Nikkei Asia)
author: Nikkei Asia
content_snippet: BENGALURU -- Recent college graduates in India could struggle to land technology jobs as companies automate entry-level coding and software testing work with artificial intelligence, the top executive at the country's largest industry body for technology companies told Nikkei Asia.
summary_en: The president of India's top tech industry body warned that AI automation is displacing entry-level coding and testing roles, making it harder for fresh grads to land jobs. He urged an immediate overhaul of CS curricula to align with the new AI-driven reality.
